# *Signal*.

:::{.callout-important}
## In Brief
Signal is the discipline of refusing to move forward until one constraint has been identified precisely, confirmed against actual numbers, and quantified in dollars or hours. By the time you finish this stage, you have a one-page constraint statement that names the problem, where it lives, how long it has existed, and what it has cost. Everything in the rest of the Sequence is designed to answer the question Signal asks.
:::

We were in our own L10 — not a client's, ours — reviewing the scorecard for our project management function. The numbers weren't red. They were worse than red. They were blank. Tasks were being created but not updated. Client deliverables were slipping by days without anyone flagging it. Billing was late because nobody could confirm what had been delivered and what hadn't. We had a project coordinator — a subcontractor we were paying $24,000 a year — and the work was still falling behind.

I asked the room a question I ask clients all the time: what is this costing us? Not the subcontractor's invoice. The actual cost — the late billing, the missed deliverables, the hours our VP of Operations was spending chasing task updates instead of running operations.

Nobody had the number. We'd been living with the problem long enough that it felt like weather — just the way project coordination worked at our size. The coordinator was failing — but the role was also inadequate. The work required someone to be in the system all day, every day, updating tasks, sending reminders, flagging overdue items, generating reports. No part-time subcontractor was going to sustain that, and hiring a full-time person meant $50,000 or more for work that was largely mechanical.

The real question was whether this was a capacity problem, a capability problem, or whether we could redesign the work itself. Is the coordinator behind because there aren't enough hours? Because they lack the skill? Or because the work shouldn't be structured this way at all? That question — *is this about adding more hours, finding a better person, or changing how the work gets done?* — is what launched us down the path that became Source and Design.

That conversation was the first time we named the constraint instead of describing the symptom. The symptom was "tasks are falling behind." The constraint was structural: the project coordination function required constant, systematic attention that no human in the role — at the price point we could justify — was going to sustain. Signal is the discipline that makes that distinction possible. Most teams never make it. They replace the person, or add a person, or build a workaround — and the constraint stays exactly where it was.

## The deliverable is *one sentence*.

Signal produces a single artifact: a one-page constraint statement anchored in one sentence. The sentence carries the constraint — the problem, where it lives in the org, how long it has existed, and what it has cost in dollars, time, or margin. The page surrounds it with the evidence that validates it: the data you checked, the people you talked to, the number you confirmed.

Here's the template. You'll fill it in by the end of this chapter.

{{< excalidraw ch04-constraint-statement-template "Constraint statement template: one sentence, location, duration, quantified cost, and validating evidence." >}}

The discipline of insisting on one is the entire point. Most leadership teams arrive at this conversation with five candidates and a tendency to argue for whichever one is loudest in the room that week. The job of Signal is to refuse the list. You pick one — the constraint that, if removed, would change the math most meaningfully — and you commit to it for the length of the Sprint.

That commitment is structural. A Sprint that tries to solve three problems solves none of them. A Sprint that solves one produces a measurable result against a number you wrote down at the start, and that result becomes the proof point that earns the next Sprint. The narrowness is what makes the work pay.

The quantified cost is non-negotiable. "It's a big problem" is not a Signal. "The quoting bottleneck is costing us $558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor underutilization" is. The number does two things. It tells you whether the constraint is worth a Sprint's attention, and it gives you a target the Deliver phase can measure against. Without it, you cannot prove the Sprint paid for itself.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
If you can't put a number on the cost, you haven't found the constraint yet. Keep working. "Significant" is not a number. Neither is "a lot." Hours per week, dollars per quarter, margin lost, deals not closed — pick a unit and estimate it.
:::

## The gate is real. You don't get past it by *declaring* it complete.

Signal is a gate. You don't move to Source until the constraint is locked — one validated constraint statement with a number on it.

The most common failure mode is political, not technical. Leadership teams can't agree on which constraint is the constraint, so they punt — they pick three, or they write something so abstract it can't be acted on. If your team can't pick one, you've learned something important before a single line of the Sprint has been built: the leadership team is unclear about priorities. That's upstream of anything in this book.

When a team does land on one constraint and commits to it, you're no longer arguing about the surface of the problem. You're arguing about the math of solving it. That's the moment Signal is locked.

## *Symptom* is not the same as *constraint*.

Most organizations bring symptoms to the table. "Our quoting takes too long." "Our onboarding is messy." These are real, and the people raising them are not wrong — but neither of them, as stated, is a constraint a Sprint can solve.

Signal traces the symptom to the underlying constraint. Quoting takes too long because three different systems hold pieces of the customer record, and the ops manager is the only person who knows how to reconcile them. Onboarding is messy because the handoff between sales and delivery is undefined, and every new customer triggers a custom escalation chain.

Consider Meridian Manufacturing — the fictional composite we introduced earlier. The symptom their team brought to the table: "Our quoting takes too long." The constraint underneath it: Elena Ruiz, the VP of Operations, was the sole quoting bottleneck. Every quote passed through her because she was the only person who held the customer-specific pricing, material lead-time knowledge, and historical job context simultaneously. The cost: $558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor underutilization. That is the difference between a symptom and a constraint. The symptom describes what you feel. The constraint names the structural cause — and puts a number on it.

Signal makes you stop at the symptom long enough to find the constraint underneath it — and then makes you put a number on what that constraint is costing. Until both moves are complete, you are not at Signal yet. You are still describing the weather.

### The Is/Is Not test.

One of the fastest ways to separate a symptom from a constraint is the Is/Is Not test. For each candidate that feels important, fill in four rows:

| | IS | IS NOT |
|---|---|---|
| **Where** does it occur? | (specific team, workflow, handoff) | (teams/workflows where it doesn't appear) |
| **When** does it happen? | (triggers, timing, conditions) | (conditions where it doesn't happen) |
| **Who** is affected? | (specific roles, customers) | (roles/customers who don't experience it) |
| **What** is the problem? | (precise description) | (what it is NOT — related problems that are different) |

The pattern that emerges from the IS NOT column is often more diagnostic than the IS column. If the problem occurs in quoting but not in invoicing, the constraint lives in the quoting workflow specifically — not in "operations" broadly. The negative space tells you where the boundary is.

### The Five Whys.

Once you've narrowed the location, trace the symptom to root cause:

1. Why is this happening? (first answer — usually a symptom)
2. Why is that the case? (gets closer)
3. Why does that occur? (starts touching the constraint)
4. What's beneath that? (structural cause)
5. What's the root cause? (the constraint itself)

**Stop rule:** You've reached the constraint when the answer points to a workflow, a handoff, a missing system, or a structural gap — not a person's behavior or a market condition.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
If your fifth "why" points to a person — "because Sarah is the only one who knows" — reframe. The constraint is not Sarah. It's the fact that critical knowledge lives in one person's head with no system to distribute it.
:::

With the Is/Is Not test and Five Whys in hand, you have what you need to separate your real constraints from the symptoms surrounding them.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Pick your top three candidates. Run Is/Is Not on each. Then run Five Whys on the survivors. Cross off anything that traces to a market condition, a personality, or a problem you can't put a number on.
:::

## The PT clinic that almost opened a sixth location.

I sat in on a meeting with a PT clinic operator that was forty-five minutes into a conversation about opening their sixth location. Site selection, lease terms, staffing — everyone around the table owned a piece of the vision. Nobody was wrong, exactly. They were just solving the wrong problem.

I asked what their clinical efficiency rating was across the five clinics they already had. The room went quiet. Not uncomfortable quiet — confused quiet, like I'd asked a question in a language they almost spoke. Nobody knew. I walked to the whiteboard, drew the formula, and we calculated it together. The number came out between 58 and 63 percent depending on the location. Industry standard for expansion is 83.

{{< excalidraw ch04-efficiency-gap "Clinical efficiency gap: actual 58–63% vs. expansion threshold of 83%." >}}

I put the marker down and said: we've spent four hours today discussing a sixth facility, and the five you already own are running at 60 percent efficiency. You're not ready to expand. Stop that conversation.

The room agreed. That's the moment Signal locks. Not the insight — the agreement. The whole conversation turned. What was the constraint underneath the efficiency gap? Scheduling. When patients canceled, nobody filled those slots fast enough. The front desk was running the replacement loop manually — checking the waitlist in the EHR, calling patients one by one, hoping someone could come in on short notice. A backlog of people who wanted appointments existed in the system. The process connecting them to the open slots was broken. Thirty-seven to forty-two percent of cancellation slots went unfilled, despite a waitlist of patients who wanted those appointments.

The expansion plan was a symptom. The scheduling loop was the constraint. The gap between 60 and 83 is the number that tells you which one to work on.

Here's what the one-page constraint statement looked like for that clinic:

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Constraint** | Patient cancellation slots are filled manually by front desk staff, leaving 37-42% of slots unfilled despite a backlog of patients waiting for appointments. |
| **Where it lives** | Front desk → scheduling workflow → manual process of matching cancellations to the waitlist. All 5 locations. |
| **Duration** | ~2 years (since third location opened). Workaround normalized — staff treats manual slot-filling as their job, not as a broken process. |
| **Quantified cost** | Efficiency at 58-63% vs. 83% expansion threshold. ~$420K/year in unrealized revenue (22 unfilled slots/week x $75 avg visit x 5 locations x 50 weeks). Blocking planned 6th location — est. $200K+ in delayed expansion revenue. |
| **Validating evidence** | Efficiency calculated live in leadership meeting. Front desk confirmed manual process. Waitlist exists in EHR but not connected to cancellation notifications. No staff member disputed the gap. |

That's the artifact. Anybody in that company could read it and understand what the Sprint was solving without asking a follow-up question.

## How to run Signal yourself.

Signal is a facilitated conversation. You can run it with your leadership team in a single working session — two to three hours the first time, faster once the pattern is familiar.

### Step 1: Surface the candidates.

Before you can pick one constraint, you need an honest inventory of what's broken or slow. This is the Issue Surfacer conversation. Ask the room:

1. What are we working around? What manual process exists because something upstream failed?
2. What does a new person always find confusing in their first ninety days?
3. What process would we never let a customer watch?
4. Where do we keep losing the same person or role? Turnover clusters around constraints.
5. What conversation keeps coming up in meetings but never gets resolved?

Write everything down without filtering. Aim for five to ten candidates. If you have fewer than three, you haven't been honest enough. If you have more than fifteen, you're listing symptoms — group them.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Open a whiteboard or shared doc. Spend twenty minutes listing candidates using the five questions above. No filtering, no debate about whether something belongs. Write everything down.
:::

### Step 2: Trace symptoms to constraints.

Most of your candidates are symptoms. Run the Is/Is Not test and the Five Whys (described above) on your top three. Cross off anything that traces to a market condition, a personality conflict, or a problem you can't quantify.

### Step 3: Run the five constraint questions.

Walk each surviving candidate through these five questions, in order. Do not skip ahead.

**Question 1: What is the problem in one sentence?** Force precision. "Our quoting process is slow" is not a sentence — it's a complaint. "The VP of Operations is the sole bottleneck for quoting — every quote requires her direct involvement, resulting in 3-5 day turnaround versus the 24-48 hour industry standard, costing $558K per year" is a sentence. Test: could someone outside your company read this sentence and understand the problem without a follow-up question?

**Question 2: Where does it live in the organization?** Name the team, the workflow, and the handoff. If it crosses departments, name the boundary where the breakdown occurs. Test: could you walk to the place in your building where this problem lives?

**Question 3: How long has it existed?** Months? Years? Since a system change? Since a departure? Duration tells you two things: how deeply embedded the workarounds are, and whether the team has normalized the problem. Anything over twelve months has almost certainly been normalized.

**Question 4: What does it cost?** In hours per week, dollars per quarter, margin lost, or deals not closed. This must be a number. This is the gate. Most leadership teams stop at question three — they name the problem, locate it, and jump to solutions. The quantified cost is what turns a complaint into a constraint you can act on.

If the data isn't clean, estimate:

- **Hours:** "How many hours per week does this person or team spend on this?" multiplied by hourly loaded cost, multiplied by 52 weeks.
- **Deals:** "How many quotes or opportunities did we lose or not pursue because of this?" multiplied by average deal value.
- **Margin:** "What would our margin be on this line if this constraint didn't exist?" minus current margin.
- **Speed:** "How many days does this add to our cycle?" multiplied by cost of delay per day.

**Question 5: If this constraint were removed, what would actually change?** Be specific. Not "things would be better." What would be different in the next ninety days? Who would feel it? What number would move? Test: if someone handed you a magic wand that removed this constraint overnight, could you describe what Monday morning would look like differently?

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
Question 4 is where Signal lives or dies. "$558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor underutilization — concentrated in the quoting workflow" is Signal. "It's expensive" is not. The number tells you whether the constraint is worth a Sprint, and gives the Deliver phase a target to measure against.
:::

### Step 4: Pick one. Lock it.

When you've walked the candidates through all five questions, one will have the strongest answers — the clearest location, the longest history, the largest cost. That is the constraint you bring to Source. Write it in a single sentence, surrounded by the evidence that validates it, using the one-page template from earlier in this chapter.

Read the completed statement back to the room. Ask: "Is this the thing?" If anyone hesitates, you're not locked. Keep refining until the room agrees — not politely, but actually.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Fill in the one-page constraint statement template for your chosen constraint. Read it aloud to the team. If the room can't agree that this is the one constraint worth a Sprint, you're not done. Keep working until you have real agreement — the kind where people nod because the math convinced them, not because the meeting has gone long.
:::

### Step 5: Run the failure mode checklist.

Before you call Signal complete, check for these common failure modes:

- **Too abstract.** "We need better processes" is not a constraint. Can you point to a specific workflow?
- **Too many.** You wrote down three constraints. Pick one. A Sprint that solves three problems solves none.
- **No number.** The cost field is empty or says "significant." Go back to question four.
- **Loudest voice won.** The constraint was named by the most senior person in the room and nobody pushed back. Ask: "Did we pick this because the data points here, or because [name] said it first?"
- **Solved the symptom.** Your constraint sentence describes what you feel, not what causes it. Run Five Whys one more time.
- **Can't be solved by a Sprint.** The constraint is "our market is shrinking" or "our founder won't delegate." These are real, but they're upstream of this book. Signal is for operational constraints a Sprint can address.

If any of these are true, go back. The gate is real. Passing through it with a bad constraint statement costs more than the time it takes to fix it.

## Where the constraint comes from inside an *EOS or Scaling Up shop*.

If your company runs on EOS, Scaling Up, or a similar cadence-based management system, you already have most of Signal's inputs sitting on a whiteboard or in a shared doc. You just have to know where to look — and then run the constraint questions against what you find. (If your team hasn't yet built the muscle of identifying and articulating issues, Mark O'Donnell's *Issues!* is the place to start. Read that first, then come back here.)

**The issues list** is the most obvious input. Every L10, every weekly tactical, every quarterly review produces a list of issues the team has been carrying. Most of them are symptoms. A few of them, traced honestly, are constraints. Walk that list and ask, for each one: is this the thing, or is this how the thing shows up? When you find one that survives that question — one you can locate in a specific workflow, with a duration and a cost — run the five constraint questions against it. That becomes your constraint candidate.

**Stalled rocks** are the second input. A rock that has been carried for three quarters without progress is almost always sitting on top of a constraint that nobody named. The rock is the symptom. The constraint is whatever is preventing the rock from moving. Ask: what would have to be true for this rock to move on its own? The answer to that question is usually the constraint.

**The headcount conversation** is the third — and the most expensive to miss. Every time the org reaches for a hire, a constraint is hiding underneath. The work is real. The team is stretched. The default move is to add a person. But under that conversation is a workflow that was never designed for the volume it's now carrying. Before you post the role, run the constraint questions: what is the constraint generating the demand for a new hire? Where does it live? What has it cost this quarter? Half the time, naming it changes what you do next. The other half, you still hire — but against a redesigned workflow rather than the one that's already failing.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Pull your current issues list, your stalled rocks, and any open headcount requests. Pick the one that feels most expensive and run it through the five constraint questions. If you can put a real number on it, you have a constraint worth a Sprint. If you can't, keep walking the list.
:::

## The failure mode that looks like work.

Skipping Signal doesn't look like failure. It looks like procrastination dressed up as activity — tools being evaluated, demos on Fridays, somebody prompting in Slack. None of it is Signal. The org hasn't named a single constraint it's committed to solving.

Watch for the version that shows up in well-run EOS shops: the leadership team sits down to work through the issues list. Someone with authority names the problem. The room nods. They move to solutions. Nobody asks whether the named problem is actually the problem. That's not Signal. It's a performance of Signal. The dominant personality resolved the discomfort of ambiguity, and the underlying constraint is still there, unnamed, costing the same amount it was costing before the meeting started.

## With the constraint locked, you can map *what surrounds it*.

The one-page constraint statement is the handoff to Source. With the constraint named, quantified, and validated, the next move is to map the knowledge and data that surround it — what the organization actually knows about the problem, where that knowledge lives, who holds it, and what is missing.

If you can't hand someone that one page and have them understand what the Sprint is solving without asking a follow-up question, you're not done with Signal. Go back. The gate is real.

That is Chapter 5.

## Reflection Questions

1. Run the Issue Surfacer questions on your company right now: what process would you never let a customer watch? Where does your team keep losing the same person or role? What conversation keeps coming up in L10s but never gets resolved? Which answer feels most expensive?
2. The PT clinic was forty-five minutes into planning a sixth location before someone asked what clinical efficiency rating was. Where in your company is your team solving a symptom while the actual constraint runs untouched underneath it?
3. Apply the Five Whys to your top constraint candidate. Does the fifth "why" point to a workflow, a handoff, or a structural gap — or does it point to a person? If it points to a person, reframe: what system failure put that person in the position of being the only one who knows?
4. Can you fill in all four fields of the one-page constraint statement template today — constraint sentence, location, duration, and quantified cost with math? If the cost field is empty, what data would you need to fill it in, and who owns that data?
5. If you polled your leadership team individually and asked "what is the ONE operational problem AI should solve for us?" — how many different answers would you get? Run the poll before your next L10 and compare results.
